title: The first fork: upper or lower motor neuron
description: How tone and reflexes separate an upper from a lower motor neuron lesion, where those rules bend, and how the same reasoning sorts the floppy infant.
why: Deciding whether weakness comes from the upper or the lower motor neuron is the first and most powerful split in localization, and the examination usually makes it within minutes.
objectives: Distinguish upper from lower motor neuron lesions by distribution, wasting, tone and reflexes.
Tell spasticity from rigidity, and place hypotonia on the reflex arc.
Grade reflexes, judge clonus, and recognize a true extensor plantar response at any age.
Recognize when the usual signs mislead: neural shock, early cerebral palsy, axonal Guillain-Barré syndrome, the face.
Decide whether a floppy infant's hypotonia is central or peripheral.

sections.title: Why the two motor neurons fail in opposite ways
sections.content:
Damage the nerve that runs to a muscle and its reflex fades away, yet damage the pathway from the brain that controls the same muscle and the reflex grows livelier than before. The reason is that every voluntary movement passes through two neurons in series. The **upper motor neuron** begins in the cortex and runs down through the brain, brainstem and spinal cord. The **lower motor neuron** begins in the anterior horn of the cord or in a cranial nerve nucleus, leaves in a root and a nerve, and ends at the muscle. Pearl and Emsellem draw the boundary at the synapse on the anterior horn cell, so that a lesion anywhere above it is an upper motor neuron lesion and a lesion of the motor unit, from the anterior horn to the muscle, is a lower motor neuron lesion (Pearl 2014, p. 65). Because the two kinds of lesion produce opposite signatures, this is the first and most powerful fork in localization, and you can usually tell them apart within minutes.

**Why the signs come out opposite**

The lower motor neuron is the final common path to muscle, so when it is cut the muscle loses its nerve. It weakens, wastes early and severely, and may twitch with fasciculations, and because the reflex arc it belongs to is broken, the reflexes fall and tone drops. The upper motor neuron mostly modulates the lower one, which includes holding its reflex activity in check. When the upper neuron is cut, the lower neuron is still alive and is now **released**, which is why the reflexes become brisk, tone rises, clonus may appear and the plantar response turns upward (Pearl 2014, p. 65).

DeMyer sets the two side by side in a table (DeMyer, p. 289).
- **Distribution.** Upper motor neuron lesions weaken *movements*, in a hemiplegic, quadriplegic or paraplegic pattern, rather than individual muscles. Lower motor neuron lesions weaken *individual muscles*, or groups of them in the distribution of a root or nerve.
- **Wasting.** Upper motor neuron lesions cause only disuse atrophy, late and slight, while lower motor neuron lesions cause early, severe denervation atrophy with fasciculations.
- **Reflexes and tone.** Upper motor neuron lesions bring brisk reflexes, clonus, clasp-knife spasticity and an extensor plantar response, and lower motor neuron lesions bring reduced or absent reflexes with hypotonia.

> **Bedside trick.** Ask the child to hold both arms straight out with the palms up and the eyes closed, like a waiter carrying two trays. An arm that turns palm down and sinks is showing pronator drift, which can reveal a subtle hemiparesis (Pearl 2014, p. 145). It works because it tests a held posture of the whole limb, which suits a lesion that weakens movements rather than single muscles (DeMyer, p. 289).

**Try the full localizer above.** Switch on brisk reflexes and every level of the motor unit disappears. Switch on absent reflexes instead and the brain and brainstem disappear, though the cord survives, for reasons the next sections explain. A single well-chosen sign has taken half the nervous system out of consideration.

In a child the fork works the same way, but sections 4 and 5 develop two warnings. An acute or early upper motor neuron lesion can look floppy, and in infancy hypotonia is far more often central than peripheral.
keyPoints: The upper motor neuron runs from the cortex to its synapse on the anterior horn cell, and the lower motor neuron runs from the anterior horn to the muscle (Pearl 2014, p. 65).
An upper motor neuron lesion releases the lower neuron, producing brisk reflexes, spasticity, clonus and an upgoing toe.
A lower motor neuron lesion denervates the muscle, producing early wasting, fasciculations, reduced reflexes and hypotonia.
Upper motor neuron lesions weaken movements in hemiplegic, paraplegic or quadriplegic patterns, while lower motor neuron lesions weaken muscles in the pattern of a root or nerve (DeMyer, p. 289).

question.question: A 13-year-old has had six months of weakness in the right hand. The small hand muscles are visibly wasted and twitch with fasciculations, the right triceps and finger reflexes are absent, tone is low, and both plantar responses are flexor. Which side of the first fork does this belong to?
options: An upper motor neuron lesion in the left motor cortex
A lower motor neuron lesion somewhere in the motor unit supplying the right hand
An upper motor neuron lesion in the corticospinal tract of the cervical cord
Neither, because the fork cannot be decided without imaging
question.explanation: Early wasting, fasciculations, lost reflexes and low tone confined to a group of muscles make up the denervation signature of a lower motor neuron lesion (DeMyer, p. 289; Pearl 2014, p. 65). What remains open is which part of the motor unit is responsible (anterior horn, root, plexus or nerve), and later modules take that up. A lesion in the left motor cortex would weaken movements of the whole arm, with brisk reflexes and little wasting. A corticospinal tract lesion in the cervical cord would make the reflexes brisk below the level of damage instead of abolishing them. Imaging has its place, but it comes after localization, and here the examination has already chosen the fork.

sections.title: Tone: spasticity, rigidity and hypotonia
sections.content:
Before you can recognize abnormal tone in a child, it helps to know what normal tone feels like, and DeMyer suggests learning it on yourself. Rest one forearm on your thigh with the wrist dangling, relax it completely, and move the wrist with your other hand. The faint resistance you feel is normal **tone**, the slight resistance of a relaxed joint to passive movement, and the limits of the range are set by the ligaments (DeMyer, p. 270). Every abnormality of tone is some departure from that feeling, and the *kind* of departure is what localizes.

**Spasticity and rigidity, and why speed matters**

DeMyer separates the two by the speed of the movement that brings them out (DeMyer, p. 273).
- **Spasticity** appears when you move the limb **quickly**. You feel a catch and then a give, which is the clasp-knife phenomenon, and it follows the distribution of an upper motor neuron lesion, whether hemiplegic, paraplegic or quadriplegic.
- **Rigidity** appears when you move the limb **slowly**. The resistance is uniform through the whole range, like bending a lead pipe, often with cogwheeling and a tremor at rest, and it usually affects all four limbs. It points to the basal ganglia instead of the corticospinal tract.

Tone is therefore worth testing twice, once slowly and once with a quick flick. Resistance that depends on velocity is spasticity, while resistance that is there whatever the speed is rigidity.

**Hypotonia can arise anywhere along the reflex arc**

Low tone tells you less on its own. Muscle tone depends on a whole reflex arc made up of the muscle spindle, the sensory fibers in the dorsal root, the anterior horn cell and its axon, and the muscle itself, and a break in any one of those links lets tone fall. DeMyer's table separates the peripheral causes by the company they keep (DeMyer, p. 266).
- A **dorsal root** lesion lowers tone and reflexes and causes sensory loss, without weakness or wasting.
- A **lower motor neuron** lesion adds weakness, wasting and fasciculations, without sensory loss.
- A **myopathy** gives weakness, wasting and hypotonia without fasciculations or sensory loss.

The dorsal root's part in tone has a pediatric echo. Cutting selected dorsal roots reduces tone by removing excitatory sensory inflow, and that is the reason dorsal rhizotomy is used to reduce tone in some children with spasticity (DeMyer, p. 273).

**In a child**

Tone in infants changes with age. The term newborn lies flexed, and that tight flexor tone has eased by about three months ([Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam](https://neurologicexam.med.utah.edu/pediatric/html/03month.html)). Hypotonia in an infant is also most often **central**, a point section 5 develops. Dystonia, a fourth kind of increased tone, belongs to the basal ganglia and is covered in [[m08-loops|Module 8]].
keyPoints: Tone is the slight resistance of a relaxed joint to passive movement (DeMyer, p. 270).
Spasticity depends on velocity, with a catch and yield on quick movement, and follows an upper motor neuron pattern (DeMyer, p. 273).
Rigidity is present with slow movement as well, as lead-pipe or cogwheel resistance, and points to the basal ganglia (DeMyer, p. 273).
Hypotonia can arise anywhere along the reflex arc, and companions such as sensory loss, fasciculations and wasting tell the levels apart (DeMyer, p. 266).
In infants, flexor tone loosens over the first months, and hypotonia is usually central.

question.question: In a 7-year-old, moving the elbow slowly meets almost no resistance, but a quick extension produces a sudden catch that then gives way. The same arm is weak and its reflexes are brisk. What kind of tone is this, and where does it point?
options: Rigidity, pointing to the basal ganglia
Hypotonia, pointing to the motor unit
Spasticity, pointing to an upper motor neuron lesion
Normal tone in an anxious child
question.explanation: Resistance that appears only with a quick movement and then yields is the catch-and-yield of spasticity, and together with weakness and brisk reflexes in the same arm it signals an upper motor neuron lesion (DeMyer, p. 273). Rigidity would be felt during slow movement as well, evenly through the whole range, so the near absence of resistance on slow testing rules it out. Hypotonia would offer less resistance at every speed and, if peripheral, would come with reduced reflexes. Anxiety can stiffen a limb, but it does not produce a reproducible catch that depends on velocity, and it does not explain weakness with brisk reflexes.

sections.title: Reflexes and the plantar response
sections.content:
How brisk does a reflex have to be before it counts as abnormal? The answer matters less than you might expect, because absolute briskness varies from person to person and many healthy children have lively reflexes. What the reflex hammer tests is a circuit that runs from the muscle spindle to the spinal cord and back, under the restraining hand of the upper motor neuron. A **brisk** reflex suggests that the brake is off and an **absent** one suggests that the circuit itself is broken, but the finding that carries the most weight is **asymmetry**. A difference between the two sides that reappears on repeated testing is much harder to explain away than a pair of lively knees. DeMyer recommends grading reflexes on a scale from 0 to 4+, so that findings can be compared over time and between examiners (DeMyer, p. 36), and he adds a consistency check. When the reflexes are increased on one side because of an upper motor neuron lesion, the examiner should also find weakness on that side (DeMyer, p. 268).

**Clonus**

Clonus is a rhythmic to-and-fro oscillation set off by a quick stretch, and it is another way in which hyperactive reflexes show themselves after the upper motor neuron has been interrupted. A few beats can be normal, which is called abortive clonus, and in mature individuals only **sustained** clonus counts as abnormal. Yet some normal newborns show sustained clonus, set off by movement or by gravity (DeMyer, p. 269), so the meaning of the sign depends on the age of the child in front of you.

**What makes a toe "upgoing"**

The extensor plantar response, the Babinski sign, is the most famous sign in neurology and one of the most often misread. DeMyer lists four features of a true extensor toe sign (DeMyer, pp. 281-282).
1. The toe begins to extend only after the stroke has traveled some distance along the sole.
2. It stays extended while the stroke continues.
3. When the stroke stops, it floats slowly back to neutral.
4. It is accompanied by a flexion withdrawal of the leg.

DeMyer also insists that there is **no "negative Babinski"**, because the sign is either present or absent (DeMyer, p. 281). And even a true extensor response is not always permanent, since it can appear transiently in toxic-metabolic coma or after a seizure (DeMyer, p. 282).

**In infants**

An upgoing toe is normal in the first year of life, while the corticospinal tracts are myelinating ([Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam](https://neurologicexam.med.utah.edu/pediatric/html/newborn_n.html)), and DeMyer notes that the infant's toe response varies with the kind of stimulus used (DeMyer, p. 282). At 12 months the toe may go either up or down, and what matters then is **reproducible asymmetry** ([Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam](https://neurologicexam.med.utah.edu/pediatric/html/12month.html)). If the child is ticklish, stroke the outer edge of the foot instead (DeMyer, p. 616).
keyPoints: Grade reflexes from 0 to 4+ (DeMyer, p. 36), and give reproducible asymmetry more weight than absolute briskness.
Brisk reflexes on one side from an upper motor neuron lesion should come with weakness on that side (DeMyer, p. 268).
Only sustained clonus is abnormal in mature individuals, and normal neonates may have sustained clonus (DeMyer, p. 269).
A true extensor toe starts after the stroke has moved, stays up, floats back and comes with flexion of the leg, and there is no such thing as a negative Babinski (DeMyer, pp. 281-282).
An upgoing toe is normal in the first year, and at 12 months it is asymmetry that matters (Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam).

question.question: An anxious 9-year-old's big toe jerks up the instant your key touches the sole, and he pulls his whole foot away, laughing. When you re-test with a slow stroke along the outer edge of the foot, both toes go down. How should you record the plantar responses?
options: Flexor on both sides, because the first response was a withdrawal and not an extensor sign
Extensor on both sides, because the toe went up the first time
Equivocal, with a request for an MRI of the spine
Negative Babinski on both sides
question.explanation: A true extensor response begins only after the stroke has moved along the sole, stays up while the stroke continues and floats back once it stops (DeMyer, pp. 281-282). A toe that jerks up the instant the key touches, together with withdrawal of the foot and laughter, is a ticklish withdrawal, and re-testing from the lateral edge of the foot, which DeMyer recommends for ticklish children (DeMyer, p. 616), has shown flexor responses. Recording the first response as extensor mistakes withdrawal for the sign, and a clean flexor re-test leaves no reason for imaging. 'Negative Babinski' is a term DeMyer rejects, since the sign is either present or absent (DeMyer, p. 281).

sections.title: When the rules mislead
sections.content:
The upper and lower motor neuron signatures are reliable enough to build a curriculum on, yet anyone who treats them as laws will sooner or later be humbled by a patient. Four exceptions matter most, and three of them matter especially in children.

**1. Shock, an upper lesion that looks lower**

Immediately after an acute, severe upper motor neuron lesion, the patient may be flaccid and areflexic, a stage DeMyer calls **neural shock** (spinal or cerebral, depending on the site). Brisk reflexes, spasticity and an upgoing toe emerge only as recovery begins (DeMyer, pp. 273-274). In the first days, then, a child with acute transverse myelitis or a spinal cord injury can look like a child with a peripheral neuropathy, and what keeps the cord on your list is the sensory level and the early loss of bladder control. Upper motor neuron lesions that evolve slowly behave differently, usually showing brisk reflexes and spasticity from the start without passing through a floppy phase (DeMyer, p. 274).

**2. The floppy infant who will become stiff**

DeMyer notes that infants with cerebral palsy may be hypotonic when they first present, before spasticity evolves, and that some stay hypotonic (DeMyer, p. 273). A central lesion in an infant therefore does not always announce itself with brisk reflexes. As section 5 shows, low tone with normal or brisk reflexes, depressed alertness and comparatively good limb strength should turn your thinking toward a central cause.

**3. A peripheral disorder that keeps its reflexes**

Guillain-Barré syndrome typically brings ascending flaccid weakness with areflexia. In some patients with the axonal form, however, the reflexes are preserved or even brisk, and the clinical distinction between neuropathy and myelopathy then becomes hard enough that nerve conduction studies have to settle it (DeMyer, p. 290).

**4. The face**

Students are taught that a central, upper motor neuron facial palsy spares the forehead because the forehead receives input from both hemispheres, whereas a peripheral, lower motor neuron palsy weakens the whole face. The distinction is useful, although Pearl and Emsellem call the strict version of the teaching more dogmatic than truth. Anatomical studies suggest a gradient, in which the forehead receives *less* cortical input rather than more (Pearl 2014, p. 49), so forehead sparing is best treated as a strong hint that still falls short of proof.

**When one sign disagrees**

When a single sign contradicts the rest of the picture, it is more useful to ask what could make that one sign lie than to throw away the whole pattern. The usual culprits are the time since onset, the age of the nervous system and the kind of axonal injury.
keyPoints: An acute, severe upper motor neuron lesion can be flaccid and areflexic at first, the stage of neural shock (DeMyer, pp. 273-274).
Slowly evolving upper motor neuron lesions show spasticity and brisk reflexes from the start (DeMyer, p. 274).
Infants with cerebral palsy may be hypotonic before spasticity appears (DeMyer, p. 273).
The axonal form of Guillain-Barré syndrome can preserve reflexes, and nerve conduction studies decide (DeMyer, p. 290).
Forehead sparing in a central facial palsy is a strong hint rather than a law (Pearl 2014, p. 49).

question.question: A 12-year-old woke with weak, floppy legs that worsened over a day. Knee and ankle reflexes are absent, the toes are mute, he cannot feel a pin below the umbilicus, and he has not passed urine since the morning. What is the most likely level?
options: The peripheral nerves, because the reflexes are absent
The spinal cord, in spinal shock
The muscles, because the legs are floppy
Both cerebral hemispheres
question.explanation: Absent reflexes would ordinarily point to the motor unit, but a sensory level on the trunk and early urinary retention can only come from the spinal cord. For hours to days after an acute, severe cord lesion, spinal shock leaves the legs flaccid and areflexic, and the upper motor neuron signs appear later (DeMyer, pp. 273-274). A neuropathy would explain the reflexes but cannot produce a sensory level or early retention. Muscle disease causes no sensory loss at all, and lesions of the hemispheres do not produce a level on the trunk. This child needs an urgent MRI of the spine.

sections.title: The floppy infant: central or peripheral?
sections.content:
No problem in child neurology tests the first fork more often than the floppy infant, and it begins with two words that are easy to blur. **Hypotonia** is reduced resistance to passive movement, while **weakness** is a reduced maximum power. The two can occur together or apart, and telling them apart is the key to localization ([Peredo 2009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19726697/)).

**Central causes are commoner**

In Peredo and Hannibal's review, central causes account for about 60 to 80% of infant hypotonia, and peripheral causes for about 15 to 30% ([Peredo 2009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19726697/)). The floppy infant is therefore more often a brain problem than a muscle problem. That seems backwards at first, until you remember that the motor unit is only one of the places where tone can fail.

**The signs that point centrally**

The same review lists the features that favor a central cause, which are a **depressed level of consciousness**, predominantly **axial** weakness, **relatively normal limb strength** despite the hypotonia, and **normal or brisk reflexes** ([Peredo 2009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19726697/)). Dysmorphic features, seizures, or poor feeding in a sleepy, disengaged baby add weight. The peripheral pattern is close to the mirror image, an alert, bright-eyed infant who cannot lift the limbs against gravity, whose reflexes are absent and whose tongue sometimes fasciculates.

**The history and examination do most of the work**

About half of infants with hypotonia are diagnosed from the history and examination alone ([Peredo 2009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19726697/)), and the localization chooses the first tests. A central picture calls for brain imaging and genetic testing, and a peripheral one calls for studies of the motor unit.

**One pattern to never miss**

Infant botulism localizes to the neuromuscular junction and is treatable, and it should be suspected in an infant under 6 months who has an acute or subacute floppy illness with constipation, listlessness, poor feeding, a weak cry and a reduced gag ([Peredo 2009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19726697/)).

**Use the presets in the figure above.** The sleepy infant with brisk reflexes leaves the brain and brainstem standing. The alert infant with tongue fasciculations and no reflexes leaves the anterior horn cell on top, which is the picture of spinal muscular atrophy. For the constipated 3-month-old with ptosis and a weak suck, the junction is the only level that fits everything. From there you can follow the trail into the motor unit in [[m04-motor-unit|Module 4]], or into the [neuromuscular disease index](/neuromuscular).
keyPoints: Hypotonia is reduced resistance to passive movement and weakness is reduced power, and the two should be assessed separately (Peredo 2009).
Central causes account for about 60 to 80% of infant hypotonia, and peripheral causes for about 15 to 30% (Peredo 2009).
Depressed consciousness, axial weakness, relatively normal limb strength and normal or brisk reflexes point to a central cause (Peredo 2009).
About half of hypotonic infants are diagnosed from the history and examination alone (Peredo 2009).
Infant botulism should be suspected under 6 months when floppiness comes with constipation, a weak cry, poor feeding and a reduced gag (Peredo 2009).

question.question: A 4-month-old is bright, smiles and follows faces, but cannot lift her arms or legs against gravity. Her reflexes are absent and her tongue quivers at rest. What is the most likely level, and what should happen next?
options: Central hypotonia, so a brain MRI should come first
The neuromuscular junction, so a trial of pyridostigmine is the next step
Muscle, so check the creatine kinase and wait
The anterior horn cell, so arrange urgent genetic testing for spinal muscular atrophy
question.explanation: An alert infant with profound limb weakness, absent reflexes and tongue fasciculations has the peripheral pattern (Peredo 2009), and fasciculations with areflexia and no sensory disorder point to the anterior horn cell. That is the picture of spinal muscular atrophy, which now has time-sensitive treatments, so genetic testing should be urgent. Central hypotonia would come with depressed alertness and preserved or brisk reflexes, the opposite of this bright, areflexic baby. Neither junction disorders nor muscle disease cause fasciculations, and waiting on a creatine kinase would lose time that matters.

quiz.question: Which combination of findings most strongly suggests a lower motor neuron lesion?
options: Weakness of a hand, early wasting, fasciculations and an absent reflex
Weakness of the whole arm, brisk reflexes and an upgoing toe
Lead-pipe rigidity in all four limbs
Ataxia with normal strength
quiz.explanation: Early denervation wasting, fasciculations and a lost reflex in a group of muscles make up the lower motor neuron signature (DeMyer, p. 289). Weakness of the whole arm with brisk reflexes and an upgoing toe is the upper motor neuron picture instead. Lead-pipe rigidity in all four limbs points to the basal ganglia, and ataxia with normal strength points to the cerebellum or its connections, so neither one implicates the motor neurons themselves.

quiz.question: A 16-year-old has brisk reflexes in the right arm and leg. On careful testing the right side is not weak at all, and on re-examination the reflexes on the left are just as brisk. How should you interpret the reflexes?
options: A left hemisphere lesion
A cervical cord lesion
Probably physiological briskness, since re-testing shows no asymmetry and there is no matching weakness
A peripheral neuropathy
quiz.explanation: Reflex briskness varies among healthy people, so what matters is asymmetry that can be reproduced, and DeMyer notes that brisk reflexes on one side from an upper motor neuron lesion should come with weakness on that side (DeMyer, p. 268). Symmetric brisk reflexes without weakness are usually physiological. A lesion of the left hemisphere or of the cervical cord would be expected to leave other signs behind, and a peripheral neuropathy lowers reflexes instead of raising them.

quiz.question: Testing a 10-year-old's ankle, you feel four beats of clonus that then stop. The other ankle behaves the same way, and there is no weakness. How should this be recorded and interpreted?
options: Sustained clonus, indicating corticospinal tract disease
Unsustained (abortive) clonus, which can occur in normal individuals
A sign of spinal cord compression requiring urgent imaging
A sign of peripheral neuropathy
quiz.explanation: A few clonic beats that die away are abortive, or unsustained, clonus, which can occur with physiological hyperreflexia, and in mature individuals only sustained clonus counts as abnormal (DeMyer, p. 269). Recording these four beats as sustained clonus misreads the finding. With no weakness, no asymmetry and no other signs there is no reason to suspect compression of the cord, and a neuropathy reduces reflexes and does not cause clonus at all.

quiz.question: Two days after a severe spinal cord injury at T6, a 14-year-old's legs are flaccid with absent reflexes. A medical student argues this proves a peripheral lesion. What is the correct response?
options: Agree, because absent reflexes always mean a lower motor neuron lesion
Agree, because the injury must also have damaged the lumbar plexus
Disagree, because flaccid legs mean a muscle injury
Disagree, because this is spinal shock and upper motor neuron signs are expected to appear as he recovers
quiz.explanation: After an acute, severe upper motor neuron lesion, a patient may pass through a stage of neural shock with flaccid paralysis and areflexia, and the reflexes, spasticity and extensor toes appear as recovery begins (DeMyer, pp. 273-274). The usual rule linking areflexia to the motor unit does not hold during that window. Nothing in the story calls for a second injury to the lumbar plexus, and flaccid legs do not by themselves point to the muscle.

quiz.question: A 2-month-old is floppy, feeds poorly and is hard to rouse, yet moves the limbs against gravity, and the reflexes are brisk. Which level of the nervous system is most likely involved?
options: The anterior horn cell
The peripheral nerves
The muscle
The brain (central hypotonia)
quiz.explanation: A depressed level of consciousness, relatively preserved limb strength and normal or brisk reflexes are the features of central hypotonia, which accounts for most hypotonia in infants (Peredo 2009). Disorders of the anterior horn cell, the peripheral nerves and the muscle produce something quite different, an alert infant with true weakness and reduced reflexes. In this baby, brain imaging and genetic testing would come first.

quiz.question: A 4-year-old has a right facial palsy in which he cannot close the right eye fully or wrinkle the right forehead, and the right arm and leg are normal. How confident can you be that this is a peripheral (lower motor neuron) facial palsy?
options: Fairly confident, since whole-face weakness with normal limbs favors a peripheral lesion, though forehead involvement is a hint rather than a law
Certain, because the forehead is always spared in central palsies
Not at all, because the face cannot be localized at the bedside
It must be central, because the eye is involved
quiz.explanation: Weakness of the whole face, forehead included, with normal limbs is the usual picture of a lower motor neuron facial palsy. Pearl and Emsellem caution, though, that the strict teaching about forehead sparing is more dogmatic than truth (Pearl 2014, p. 49), so the finding supports the localization without proving it, and saying the forehead is always spared in central palsies overstates the case. Facial weakness can certainly be localized at the bedside, and weakness of eye closure does not make a palsy central.

signOff: On five patients, classifies the weakness as upper or lower motor neuron from the examination alone, agreeing with faculty.

opener.parable: Stroke the sole of a four-month-old's foot and the big toe will often rise, which is entirely normal at that age. Do the same in a four-year-old and the identical movement tells you that something has gone wrong in the pathway coming down from the brain.
opener.history: In 1896 Joseph Babinski (1857–1932) described the big toe that rises instead of curling when the sole is stroked after damage to the upper motor neuron. He also introduced the word anosognosia, for a patient with a left hemiplegia who seemed unaware of it.
